lines.text: >> Thank you.
>> Mr. Chairman, our next case this evening is ZBA 2026-55.
This is property located 218 South Lincoln Street.
This is the R2 zoning district.
Attorney Andrew Sullivan and his agent proposed to convert a two-family dwelling to a three-family
dwelling and seeks a variance from section 4.3A1C for the multifamily dwelling.
And this is as per document submitted through June 11, 2026.
>> Before I begin my presentation, a couple handouts.
>> I sure do have one for Mike.
>> Okay.
>> Okay.
>> Okay.
>> Good evening.
My name is Andy Sullivan, attorney for Mr. Assey sitting next to me.
He owns the property through his trust.
Just to give a little background, that's why I handed out these.
He and his father and his three brothers built the property in 1958.
It's been me and/or around his family since then.
It was originally used for the whole family, but it was designed so it could seamlessly
convert into a three-family back then.
The section in the front that you see that faces Beauvoir was originally a big kitchen
and four boys, but that hasn't been used since the 1960s, and that's the area that will become
the proposed third unit.
The objective here is to convert a use that is two-family into a three-family.
The lot, as you can see from the plan, the tax map and the chart of lot sizes in the
area, it's the largest lot in the area.
The house, however, is configured such that it can't be subdivided.
Whatever happens, happens with this big lot.
It's a corner lot.
It has like 258 feet of frontage.
It just means minor dimensional deficiencies, but it meets setbacks for the most part.
The lot area, again, meets all this, but it is asking for a three-family in the zone.
Right now, there are six bedrooms, two units.
There will be only five bedrooms when it becomes a three-family.
I mentioned that because one of the objecting letters said, "Well, it's going to be six
bedrooms."
It's not.
It's actually going to be one less.
He designed the lot, you can see on the plan, which is at Appendix H, with six parking spots
under the new statutory.
You only need one per unit, he could have one per unit, but he designed it with six,
so it would ameliorate any need for offsite parking, and it fits nicely in the lot.
So if we look at the age of the building, the building exterior, it's size, its footprint
will not change.
So for the last almost 68 years, it's been a major component of the neighborhood.
It's not going to change the look of the neighborhood.
Six parking spots are provided, double the amount required.
Because it's on the corner of South Lincoln, the traffic flow to the back neighborhood,
Beauvoir, and Vinton Street, it's not going to happen.
It's all going on South Lincoln Street.
And third unit will obviously add much needed parking.
Not much needed housing stock.
Now I know Alderman Berkes wrote a letter to the board saying it's had a lot of adverse
activity there, which is absolutely true.
But one of the handouts I gave you is a vacate letter.
The place is empty.
I started an eviction proceeding.
He defaulted, but he left on the 8th, so it is completely empty.
The objective here, Mr. Assey is 95 years old, he'll probably outlive everybody in this
room.
He's in great shape.
But nonetheless, he's trying to plan ahead.
His nephew, who he's taken care of as his son probably for the last 50 years, he plans
to have him ultimately get the property, live there as soon as it's renovated.
And with the two units, that would be enough income to provide taxes maintenance and keep
it up with an owner occupied.
We all don't own occupied.
They're not going to let scumbags, dirt bags, and whatever else baggage there.
It's going to be a nice, cleanly run property.
About nine neighbors submitted positive letters that supported the two letters that were objected.
One was not in the butter, but was diagonally across the street in South Lincoln.
The other one is across the street as in the butter.
But they both talk about the use, which I'm going to call the former use of the property,
meaning it was not a great spot.
People were in there that shouldn't have been there.
They were doing things, probably they shouldn't have done.
That has all stopped.
Whatever happened in the future, I doubt it would have been owner occupied right there
keeping track of it.
That's why insurance companies, banks, laws, owner, and occupiers, they take better care
of the property.
But in terms of the variance, how it was used in the history is really not relevant, even
though, of course, subjectively we all look at it and think about it, but it's just not
going to happen again.
What is happening is we have a building that was originally designed for a three family
70 years ago, but they had a big family, didn't need it, and now they want to put it back
in there.
The largest lot in the area.
The exterior won't change except for one door being added, and it'll be the six parking
spots rather than the dirt parking lot of indeterminate number of spaces they have now.
It'll be a cleaner looking building, it'll be a cleaner looking lot.
It'll be owner occupied, and the variance relief request is very minimal.
It's a reasonable use.
In fact, the kitchen layout is still there.
It would cost more money to renovate that and make it larger, two units, two family,
than it going into a three family.
It's 90% there.
It's been 90% there for probably 70 years.
As a matter of fact, the other picture I showed you in color, it shows you there are already
three electric service panels there.
They've been there for 70 years.
There are already three, were there water pumps?
What are the three water pumps?
The other pictures?
The water pumps?
Al's gone to the death here.
What were the, what are these right here?
Oh, yeah.
They were circulated from the heating system.
So there's already three zone heating systems in place.
It's been there for 70 years.
It was designed as a three family back in '58.
So again, it's a reasonable use.
It would be a hardship to do nothing.
I mean, it's a waste of the property, and the building is designed really for a three
family.
It's a little finishing touches, and that's what he plans to do.
I have a floor plan I submitted to and how he plans to put it together.
Al's been a builder in the city for what, 80 years?
At least something like that.
He's very good at what he does, and he just needs some tender loving care and an occupied
family member to make it work.
I'm open for questions.
Thank you.
Members of the board, anyone have any questions of the applicant?
Are there any other three family units in the neighborhood?
On that side, I have a chart.
They're across the street, meaning between South Lincoln and South Will, but not on his
side.
No, they're not.
He's not in the immediate area that I scoped out.
There are two families, but it's predominantly single family.
I have a chart, an annotated chart.
I think it's A. It's exhibit C. I labeled what I found from the city records.
His is a two family.
Down the block on that street, excuse me, on Vinton Street, there are one, two, three,
two families.
Across on Lincoln, there's another three families somewhere.
Office, now you're getting more towards South Will Street, so there's retail, et cetera.
Do all the board members see that on its exhibit C of Andy's packet?
All right.
Catherine?
Can you tell me, please, about you mentioned that in the past it had a variance for three
apartments.
What year?
When was this?
We don't know.
We looked and the city said they didn't keep records that far back.
I couldn't find it either.
He thinks it was before 1965 or whatever.
Whenever the city started keeping hard records.
When were the three panels installed?
They were installed when the building was built.
It was always designed to meld into a three family when it was built.
As far as it was a builder, too.
All right.
Thank you.
Craig?
The three panels, though, it's house unit one and unit two, correct?
So you need four at a third unit?
No, there's only going to be three units.
There's three panels for that.
So each spot which will be the three family has its own separate unit.
Again, the section that will be the new third unit, that was part of the original house.
There's a kitchen in there and the kitchen layout is still there to still counter.
The one that is still plumb for that.
But you'll still need a house meter or one of the tenants or the owner occupant would
be paying the electric.
Yes, it's designed so that the media will serve the particular three units, even though
the units are going to be reconfigured.
Mr. Chairman, I just want to follow up.
Craig makes a good point.
Most multifamily buildings have a -- you know, the landlord has a house panel and that powers
all the common areas of stairwells.
And that's kind of what this seems like right now in this current instance.
Al, quick, but there's not going to be any common area.
Is there -- each unit will be self-sustained?
Common area?
No.
Each unit will be self-sustained?
Each unit will be separate.
So the service panel for each unit will serve only?
Yeah, each one has its own service and nothing changes on the outside of the building.
There's no lighting outside of the units like the hallways are pitch black all the time?
The hallways are contained within the unit.
Each unit -- so is that -- you're saying each unit is -- has its own entrance?
Yes.
Two.
Because no outside changes to the footprint except one door.
That's it.
But each unit has two accesses to the outside.
And those are contained within the unit.
So there's no common area.
There may be outside lights, but it goes with a particular unit.
And as a follow-up to that, I think -- I won't dig into that too much.
You could add a panel if you chose, of course.
But even a networked fire system should be on its own separate piece for any space where
there's common systems.
The tenants need to have access to their system.
So --
Whatever the building department wants will be done.
Sure.
I think the other question that's important when I look at this, the ownership staying
the same with ongoing, is that correct?
So I know you said that there'll be an owner-occupant.
But is the applicant moving in or is it the family member?
No, no, no.
Just his nephew.
The applicant lives elsewhere.
Okay.
So that's not owner-occupied as you're presenting?
At this point in time, no, but it will be because it will be --
Anything can or will be, but that's not what it is.
I never said it was.
That's the objective.
The objective is it's going to be conveyed to the nephew.
Okay.
So a concern I have on this is that --
If you want to make that a condition, not a problem.
The property's been allowed to get into a condition that's concerning.
So I want to understand if the same applicant's going to continue owning it as they make these
-- what was the reason that it was allowed to degrade to its current state?
The aerial photos have tarps on the roof.
As a rental property, it was allowed to get pretty blighted.
He's asking basically -- He's asking why did the property become kind of like a scum --
Why did the property get allowed to be kind of a scummer property in labor terms?
If I can hear words.
I think I carried away and I couldn't -- I always -- I kept saying they were going to
change.
I'm going to stop and I went along with them helping out their change when I happened to
throw them out.
Can you have him speaking in the microphone?
Sure.
What he's saying is he kept hearing the promises that they cleaned their act up and get better
and they kept giving away when they didn't.
But materially, so in the photos that are the aerials, there's a hole in the roof and
it's covered by a blue tarp.
That's not the tenant responsibility.
That would be an owner responsibility, correct?
Is there a hole in the roof covered with a tarp?
The tarp?
No.
And one of the older aerial photos.
There's a section we put a piece of -- That's a whole picture.
That roof was replaced last August, a year ago.
Okay.
Thank you.
You mentioned --
Yeah, that was replaced a year ago.
The nephew that's been taking care of the property as of late?
No, he's not been taking care of the property.
Al has been responsible for it but it's getting too much.
But he's going to convey the property to the nephew.
Anyone else?
We'll go to public.
Anyone here speaking in favor of this application?
Anyone to speak in opposition to the application?
Any general comments?
Any correspondences, Mike?
Yes, Mr. Chairman.
We have a letter from Alderman Jim Burkish.
He writes, I am writing today regarding proposed variance to convert the property to a three-family
dwelling.
As a result of the award, I have received numerous complaints about the condition of the property
and the activity of the tenants and visitors.
I have contacted Manchester police and city code enforcement on numerous occasions.
MPV has responded to the location 89 times in the past three-plus years for drug activity,
scrapping, noise complaints, parking issues and other homeless problems.
Code enforcement has also responded 10 times in the past year for housing code violations,
trash accumulation and people living in the shed.
Neighbors have asked me to forward their concerns as they fear retribution.
This property is negatively affecting the property values and quality of life for the
neighborhood and speaking with the owner and Alex Azy, I have advised them to rectify
the current problems and bring the property into compliance prior to seeking a variance
until these problems are rectified.
I cannot support the variance and ask the ZBA to deny Alderman James Burkish.
We have a second email here.
They write, my name is Braden McLaughlin, owner of 13 Bow
Vare Street, the single family home directly across from 218 South Lincoln Street, where
my family and I have lived since January of 2021.
I am messaging to cosign on all points the opposition letter sent by Kate Carrum, previous
to this email on 7/8/26 titled, "Objection to the proposed application of variance for
218 South Lincoln Street."
I strongly support the upholding of the denial of the appeal of forbearance in this matter,
and I will add my perspective here.
I want to first emphasize that I do not hold any ill will towards the Azy family, especially
since Alex at least has been communicative and pleasant when addressing the ongoing and
deeply problematic issues present at the property in question.
However, I must be blunt and honest throughout.
It continues to baffle me when nothing has been done about this problematic property
for years now with two separate swat raids happening over the course of my time here
and uncountable medical, fire, and police visits most recently involving a tragic overdose
death on the property.
I understand that Alex's inability to enact any lasting change regarding the illicit behavior
is in part because he was not the owner, his uncle was, and that may be changing soon and
hopefully so shall the rate of such activity may be reduced.
However, as Kate mentioned, this proposal was mentioned to me as a zero-sum game by
Alex.
There is context not noted in the application which I want to supply my subjective take
here as best I can remember with my conversation with Alex.
The ultimatum, as I understood it, was as it follows, A, either the appeal for variances
is denied and subsequently the Azzy family will freely decide to take essentially no
action at all to improve the property or situation with the current tenants or B, it is approved
and Alex's income is allegedly supported enough by additional tenants in the other two units
after evictions and repairs to live comfortably on the property.
Something he claimed to me, it would not be practical otherwise.
It is my opinion that if a person comes into possession or decision-making powers of a
property and they do not already have the financial means to live on said property without
a variance from the city, it is not the responsibility to taxpayers around them to permit a variance
so they can acquire enough passive income via landlording to support their desired lifestyle.
I am sympathetic to their desire to repair the building, rent out to law-abiding people
and restore history/sentimental altality existing here for the Azzy family, but I have doubts
as to the true level of dedication they have in helping the neighbourhood as a primary
motivator.
This is because it was implied to me that the mere possibility of a denied appeal will
threaten to stop improvements on 218 South Lincoln Street altogether and leave it as
is which leaves the surrounding neighbourhood to suffer the long-standing behaviour that
brings such tribulations such as overdoses, swat raids, drive-by dealings, manic screaming
matches resulting in police visits, roaming dilapidated RVs obstructing driveways, toxic
fumes from burning piles of unknown provenance, overflowing garbage blowing into neighbouring
yards and horrendously loud scrapyard enterprises happening on the property into the small hours.
That says to me that their interest is not focused first on improving the neighbourhood
but primarily their desire for a live-in rental property enabled by increased income by abusing
an exception to the zoning rule.
The fixing of the nuisance that is at present 218 South Lincoln Street is therefore incidental
and secondary as was implied to me to the desire to live in a restored area of the neighbourhood
with property and living off the increased landlord revenue.
They have the capability to help the neighbourhood but only on their terms.
That is their right as it is my right to voice my opposition to this unnecessary zoning exception
request.
There is no unnecessary hardship at present and it can only be reasonably used as a two-family
property as it's now zoned.
There is no reason to add a three-family building to an otherwise primarily single-family neighbourhood
beyond sheer financial gain regardless if it is for profit or for living expenses.
There is substantial research into the subject property value effects that differ from what
was stated in the application which was very little.
So I find little to trust there.
The primary ingress egress route for the cars already causes headaches for me backing out
and maneuvering around as non-residential guests frequently line Baubert Street, a short
low traffic narrow road to visit 218 South Lincoln Street.
I cannot imagine adding more residents there that would improve the situation, good intentions
or not.
Please, I will not be denied this application.
Thank you for your consideration Brady McLaughlin.
And here is the e-mail he referred to from Kate Carrum.
My name is Kate Carrum.
I'm the owner of a single-family property located at 237 South Lincoln Street.
An application has been filed by the owners of 218 South Lincoln Street for a variance.
My property is across the street from this property.
It is unclear from published records if the request has been denied but the applicant
has filed an appeal for hearings scheduled in July.
So I am going to assume that this is an ongoing request and express my strong opposition to
the applicant to request for a variance.
Under New Hampshire law and Manchester's land use code, the applicant bears the burden
of approving all five criteria for a variance.
This application feels to me four of those strict legal thresholds.
One unnecessary hardship.
The applicant has no unique hardship inherent to the land or structure itself that prevents
it from being reasonably used as a two-family home.
The property is already a functioning viable multi-family residence.
Personal financial gain or desire to maximize rental income does not legally constitute unnecessary
hardship under New Hampshire's zoning law.
Two spirit of the ordinance in public interest.
The surrounding neighborhood is characterized primarily by single-family and traditional
two-family homes.
Branding this variance would alter the essential residential character of our neighborhood,
increase density beyond what the zone intends and run contrary to the public interest.
Three, diminution of property values.
Increasing the density of this specific law will lead to a higher concentration of occupants,
increased trash management issues and heightened visual clutter.
These factors will negatively impact the aesthetics, desirability and overall market values of surrounding
properties including my own.
Four, traffic and parking congestion.
The property lacks adequate off-street parking to absorb a third residential unit.
Forcing additional vehicles onto the street creates a direct safety hazard for emergency
vehicle access, sight lines and winter snow removal.
The addition of parking spaces on the lot to accommodate a third unit will fail to provide
the required landscape buffers required for expanded parking.
All of these are disqualifying pursuant to the land use code.
In addition to failing to meet the criteria of the land use code, there were other red
flags that were causing concerns for the neighborhood.
A big part of the owner's representative pitch to the neighbors is always that there will
be a resident as well as an owner.
There is no way to guarantee that there will always be a permanent on-site resident of the
property as verbally promised.
It is not hard to envision a time when the owner moves and just rents to a third family
who sells the property outright.
There is no way to guarantee the number of tenants in a unit which he says will be two
with one child and perhaps a cat will always be enforced.
If the building would be sold with three apartments, there is no telling what the total number
of occupants could be.
All persons in three units would not be out of the question.
While we do not see how the current property can accommodate the cars for these apartments,
the owners promise that they will strictly enforce the number of cars that each of their
tenants can park on site with assigned parking.
What is the stop-off from simply parking additional cars and other vehicles on nearby public streets?
The owner's representative, Alexander Azzie, basically presented me with two options.
Either they leave the situation as it is with the building decaying and the current tenants
in place or we allow them to convert the three units which we assume is so they can maximize
revenue.
Neither of these options are acceptable.
Our property values have been negatively impact for years due to the gradual physical decay
of the residents, the increase in foot traffic, going to and from the house for the purpose
of buying and selling illegal narcotics and the all too regular police and FBI drug raids.
It is difficult to see how adding more people, more congestion, more traffic, more noise
and more transit is the solution.
I have nothing against the owners who at this time are our actual neighbors.
I appreciate that the grandson who visited me seemed sincere.
The owners could just be as sincere and simply fix the existing problems without making this
a three apartment unit building.
There is nothing stopping them from making necessary repairs and upgrades, just living
in one of the two existing apartments or selling the property.
Instead there appears to be a play to generate more rental income from the property at the
expense of the neighbors.
I strongly support the city's denial of this matter and encourage the zoning board who
once again deny this appeal, Kate Karam of 237 Lincoln Street.
That is all I have, Mr. Chairman.
>> Comment on this?
>> I will but don't you have some positive letters that I submitted?
>> With the application?
>> Yeah.
>> They are part of the record and the board has had them since you submitted this in June.
>> Okay, that's fine.
>> For the record, I mean where are they?
Attorney Sullivan.
Do you know what attachments they are?
>> I put them post application but you don't have to, you know, I just want to make sure
they are in the record.
>> We have the letter of.
>> They are all said the same thing, there are like six or seven people.
>> We see the, I think the broker opinion, I'm not.
>> I know he submitted them but that's okay.
Let me just respond.
Number one, again, it's not a metaphysical distinction but we are talking about the use
of the property, they are talking about the use of the property, so am I, versus the actual
situation at the property in terms of physical dimensions, et cetera.
Right now, it's a clean property.
No one is other than there, the outside is cleaned up, there is no hole in the roof,
so it's been cleaned up.
The question becomes will it stay that way?
Okay, will it stay that way?
The draconian alternatives that were presented by Alexander, that's the first I've heard
about it, I don't know if it's true, I don't know if it's not true, so I'm not saying first
I've heard about it.
But nonetheless, the property has been cleaned up, there is no variance yet.
So he cleaned up ahead of time, yeah, it will look good, but at the same time he made the
effort, he spent the money to get it cleaned up and get those people out of there and that's
the way they want it to stay.
Alexander is a younger guy, no offense to Mr. Asi here, but he's not.
As we all know, elderly people sometimes have difficulty exerting their will, if you will,
on other people.
It's just the nature of age.
That's not going to happen now because we have a younger guy that's going to be in charge.
He wants it cleaned, he doesn't want to live in an area like that.
So in terms of all the stuff that happened in the neighborhood because of that house,
no disagreement.
It's all a matter of fact, it's all a matter of police of record.
But it's been cleaned up, it's no different than any number of my clients who buy, beat
or apartment bills, they clean them up.
That's how they make their upside.
This upside is they want to live there, or at least Alexander wants to live there.
In terms of the character of the neighborhood, character of the neighborhood is partly how
the property is used.
It's going to be a better use of it.
But it's also what the property is going to look like.
It's going to look like it's always looked like for the last 70 years.
In terms of the parking, there's more parking than required.
We could go in and ask for just three spaces.
He purposely put six in because he realizes, as I know the plan of what it tends to do
quickly is we're not going to make you put more spaces on the lot, but you've got to
find more spaces for people to park because they're all going to have at least two cars.
I don't know if that's the case here, but there's plenty of parking.
And again, it's all going to flow into South Lincoln.
It's not going back in the neighborhood.
In terms of the property value, I have a broker's opinion of a well-known broker in the area.
Jerome Duvel says it's not going to diminish the value of the property.
I am not a broker.
But I rely on somebody else's opinion who is a broker of knowledge and skill and experience
and repute.
In terms of the hardship, it's two alternatives.
The first one is, is it a reasonable use?
It is a reasonable use.
It's a large house that was built originally to become a three-freetly.
Never did over 70 years, but it's ready for it now.
It's 90 percent there.
It would be more expensive to rip that out and make two gigantic units, which would probably
not fit the neighborhood.
It would be just too big.
Sometimes a house or an apartment is too big for the character of the neighborhood.
In this case, to have two almost 2,000 square foot -- 1,500, 1,600 square foot units in that
neighborhood probably would be too big.
That would be conducive to a larger number of people there, other than smaller three
units.
So in terms of the criteria, in the hardship, again, the lot can't be subdivided because
of the location of the house.
In a way the house is configured, it would be just an absolute waste to try to reconfigure
it than what it was originally designed for.
You don't do that.
You modify it maybe, but you don't make something bigger than it already is designed to be without
expanding the exterior.
So I think we do deference to Ms. Karamer, her name is the man across the street.
The hassle of the neighborhood, if you will, has already gone away.
It's an empty building.
It's a cleaned up lot.
What will happen tomorrow?
It will stay empty and cleaned up until it's fixed up.
He plans to fix it up.
That's what he's there for.
It's like any other guy that buys an old building, they plan to fix it up.
He plans to fix it up so a family member can live there.
He doesn't plan to live there, but a family member plans to live there and ultimately
own it.
So all that, yes, it happened, but it's not happening now.
We met all of the men's criteria.
It's cleaned up.
In terms of the other aspects, I believe we've met all the four criteria of the hardship,
and especially since the relief requested is relatively minor.
Yes, we're asking for a three family, but it's a big building.
It's a big building.
It's tailor made for a three family.
It was made for a three family.
All we're asking is to become a three family.
>> So we'll close the public.
Go ahead, Matt.
>> Could you give me a little more guidance on the hardship issue?
It seems that the zoning doesn't contemplate three units.
>> The zone is not contemplate three units.
>> The hardship, you said it's a reasonable use, but let me just ask and then give me
guidance.
But in terms of the contemplation of the zoning for that area, it isn't that they be three
family units.
>> I'm just saying it's big.
It could accommodate three units.
In ancient days, it was designed for three units.
I'm not saying it can't be shown, but I'm having a hard time seeing how either of the
two alternatives that exist for showing hardship exist.
Could you give me a little guidance on that?
>> Yes, I'm saying one of the alternatives to the hardship criteria is if it's a reasonable
use, okay, and that use can't be done without relief, that's a hardship.
It's a reasonable use to make that building into a three family, okay?
Because of its size, because it was configured that way, it's a corner lot, it's the biggest
lot in the area, that's a reasonable use.
You may disagree with that, but that is my -- I'm pausing, it's a reasonable use.
It's such a big building and a big lot.
The hardship is I can't break up the lot, so if I'm going to create that reasonable
use, I need relief.
I need relief for two reasons.
One, I can't break up the lot, can't subdivide.
Two, the build's already configured.
It's 90% there as a three family.
It's minor changes inside to make it.
Just as a question of a waste in the classical sense, it would be a hardship to waste the
value of that building.
I'm not talking about making more money, but to waste the value of the build is already
90% configured as a three family.
That's the physical hardship in conjunction with I can't subdivide a lot to create another
small 50 by 100 lot there.
So I have that physical hardship in conjunction with the reasonable use, and that meets that
criteria.
>> Great, quick.
>> So mine's not a question, more of a deliberation.
The inability to subdivide is not a hardship.
When we start looking at the pieces that I think are the most relevant here, we have
to remember that this was submitted under the old zoning.
So this is when this neighborhood was R2.
And the specific spirit of that ordinance is a mix of single and duplexes.
So when we look at the applicant's own exhibit, they've submitted that there's 41 singles,
five, two families, and one, three on their own exhibit.
So this is clearly out of the spirit of the ordinance by definition, but it's also not
in keeping with the character of this neighborhood.
And I just don't see how creating the extra unit here is meeting the spirit of that or
creating substantial justice to the neighbors that are benefiting primarily from their single
